🧵 3 AM. I'm the only ER nurse with 6 patients.

Charge yells: "Room 4 is crashing!"

At the same time:
• Room 2: Chest pain, troponin elevated
• Room 5: Post-op appy, fever 102.3
• Room 8: COPD, O2 sat 88% on 2L

Who do I see FIRST?

Room 4. "Crashing" = airway/breathing/circulation failing NOW.

After stabilizing Room 4, who NEXT?

NOT Room 2 (stable chest pain).
NOT Room 5 (fever is concerning but not crashing).

Delegate Room 8's O2 to the tech.
Reassess Room 5 from the doorway.
THEN see Room 2.

That's clinical judgment. That's the NGN. That's what I teach.

The NCLEX Next Generation isn't just a harder test — it's a fundamentally different approach to evaluating nursing competence.

After 15 years in emergency nursing and mentoring countless new grads, I've watched the transition from knowledge-based assessment to clinical judgment evaluation.

The difference:

• NEW: "Your post-op patient has K+ 5.8, BP 88/52, and says they feel 'weird.' What's your FIRST action?"

The NGN uses the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM): Recognize Cues → Analyze → Prioritize → Generate Solutions → Take Action → Evaluate.

This isn't taught in most review courses. That's why I built the Clinical Judgment Mastery System — 30+ real scenarios, decision trees, and video walkthroughs from the ER.

🧵 How to read an ABG in 4 steps (for the NCLEX and the floor):

1/ Look at the pH
< 7.35 = acidosis
> 7.45 = alkalosis

2/ Look at PaCO2
Respiratory component
Opposite direction from pH = compensation

3/ Look at HCO3
Metabolic component
Same direction as pH = primary problem

4/ Check for compensation

Is the body trying to fix it?

Example: pH 7.30, PaCO2 55, HCO3 26
→ Respiratory acidosis (pH low, CO2 high)
→ HCO3 normal = UNCOMPENSATED

🧵 The NCLEX drug calculation questions that trip up EVERYONE:

1/ Heparin drip titration

Order: 25,000 units in 500mL D5W. Start at 18 units/kg/hr. Patient weighs 70kg.

Rate = (18 x 70 x 500) / 25,000
= 630,000 / 25,000
= 25.2 mL/hr

2/ Pediatric dosing (mg/kg)

Order: Amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/day divided BID. Child weighs 22 lbs.

22 lbs / 2.2 = 10 kg
45 x 10 = 450 mg/day
450 / 2 = 225 mg per dose

3/ IV push rate

Order: Lasix 40mg IV push over 2 minutes.
Concentration: 10mg/mL

Volume = 40 / 10 = 4 mL
Rate = 4 mL / 2 min = 2 mL/min

These aren't just math. They're patient safety.

🧵 Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle — the NCLEX will test this:

1/ Measure lactate

> 2 mmol/L = tissue hypoperfusion

2/ Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics

(But don't delay antibiotics > 45 min)

3/ Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics

Within 1 hour of recognition

4/ Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4

5/ Start vasopressors if MAP < 65 after fluids

The NGN will give you a septic patient and ask:
"What's your FIRST action?"

Answer: Obtain cultures + start antibiotics. SIMULTANEOUSLY.
